title: Supply-Chain Attacks in Machine Learning Frameworks
problem: ML frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow, HuggingFace) have a larger dependency attack surface than comparable non-ML software, yet the ML community has no higher security awareness than non-ML communities, leaving ML-specific supply-chain vulnerabilities unaddressed by existing defenses.
method: Two contributions: (1) Attack demonstration - introduces ML-specific supply-chain attacks using two Python mechanisms: (a) global variable overwriting where a compromised upstream package directly mutates PyTorch/TorchVision globals (e.g., interpolation mode enums, softmax functions, model forward methods) at import time; (b) local variable overwriting using Python's inspect module and undocumented PyFrame_LocalsToFast C API to modify in-scope variables in downstream function call stacks. Three attack types demonstrated: backdoor injection via forward function hijacking, pipeline vulnerability injection via interpolation mode swap, and model weight stealing via steganographic encoding in inference outputs. (2) Security awareness analysis - LLM-assisted analysis of 549,635 GitHub issues/PRs from Top-50 ML repositories using GPT-3.5 for coarse filtering (97.8% recall) then GPT-4 for fine-grained safeguard classification (78.9% precision, 0.85 Cohen's kappa). Compared against Top-50 Linux repositories.

title: PipeFill: Using GPUs During Bubbles in Pipeline-Parallel LLM Training
problem: Pipeline-parallel LLM training leaves substantial GPU idle time (pipeline bubbles) that represents wasted compute capacity at scale.
method: PipeFill schedules independent fill jobs (batch inference, small model training) into pipeline bubble slots using a Pipeline Bubble Instruction (PBI) abstraction, a Fill Job Executor that maps fill work to idle GPU time, and a Fill Job Scheduler that tracks bubble windows and dispatches work. Implemented on DeepSpeed with GPipe and 1F1B schedules.

title: Boosting Task Scheduling Data Locality with Low-latency, HW-accelerated Label Propagation
problem: Hardware-accelerated task schedulers dispatch ready tasks to the first available core without locality awareness, causing cache misses when dependent tasks execute on different cores. Existing locality-aware policies require static programmer hints or incur high scheduling overhead incompatible with fine-grained tasks.
method: The paper introduces Task-LP, a hardware label propagation (LP) accelerator that clusters up to 128 in-flight tasks by running a semi-synchronous graph clustering algorithm on the dynamic task dependency graph built by Picos. Task-LP uses a bitmask adjacency matrix, color-iteration parallelism (First-Fit online graph coloring), and bitwise popcount to compute label popularity; it converges in under 300 cycles for typical inputs. A Task Placement Engine (TPE) combines LP cluster labels with core-idleness signals via a tunable relaxation policy (cycle-length parameter R_len) to balance locality and core utilization. The full system is prototyped on a 24-core RISC-V (Rocket Chip) mapped to an Alveo U55C FPGA, interfaced via custom RoCC instructions and the Phentos task scheduling API.

title: Stratum: System-Hardware Co-Design with Tiered Monolithic 3D-Stackable DRAM for Efficient MoE Serving
problem: MoE LLM inference is bottlenecked by the massive expert parameter volume (>95% of model size in models like Mixtral 8x7B), which overwhelms GPU HBM bandwidth and capacity; HBM-based NMP approaches are further limited by coarse-pitch TSV interconnects (~10 µm) that cap internal bandwidth.
method: Stratum integrates Mono3D DRAM with NMP logic via Cu-Cu hybrid bonding on a logic die, connected to GPU via 2.5D silicon interposer. Within the Mono3D DRAM stack, an in-memory tiering mechanism assigns expert weights to fast (low wordline-staircase latency) or slow tiers based on predicted access frequency. A lightweight topic classifier predicts which experts will be hot for a given batch of user queries and re-maps them to fast tiers before each batch via a row-swap buffer. The NMP processor on the logic die includes per-channel Processing Units (PUs) connected via a ring network, each containing near-bank PE clusters with tensor cores executing GeMM/GeMV, an intra-channel reducer, and a SIMD special-function engine for Softmax/SiLU. The prefill phase runs on the GPU (xPU) and decoding runs on Stratum NMP.

title: Radius: Range-based Gradient Sparsity for Large Foundation Model Pre-training
problem: Gradient communication in data-parallel LLM pre-training is a major bottleneck. Existing top-k sparsification methods fail with AdamW (causing divergence) and have poor scalability due to allgather operations whose cost grows linearly with worker count.
method: Radius observes that top-k gradient indices are temporally stable after 15-20% of training steps. It reuses previously computed top-k indices for T steps (T=200 default) to enable dense allreduce on only the top-k fraction of gradients (avoiding allgather). All workers use identical top-k indices (since indices are computed post-allreduce), so only the gradient values need communication without index exchange. Gradient correction (mimicking AdamW operations) is applied before index selection to select indices based on effective model updates. Error feedback accumulates non-top-k gradients for compensation at resampling steps.
